recentItems.title: Local and international artists create sculptures as part of a live showcase in Oman
recentItems.description:
(4 Sep 2026) 
OMAN SCUPLTURE SYMPOSIUM

SOURCE: ASSOCIATED PRESS

RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

LENGTH: 3:00

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Dhofar, Oman -  27 August 2026
1. Various of artist carving large-scale marble blocks 
2. Various of artists near their artworks
3. Various of Diala al-Daghlise carving large-scale marble block using a power grinder and protective gear
4. Tilt down of sculpture
5. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Diala al-Daghlise, Jordanian artist: 
“The stone is a nice material, but it's not very easy (to work with). It requires physical strength, but also thinking, engineering, and calculation. These forums are very nice because they gather people from different countries of the world to see new ideas, new ways, to know new countries. This is my first experience in the Gulf, and I am very happy that Oman was the beginning of my experience here.”

6. Artists working in open air 
7. Various of artists sanding marble 
8.  Salem al-Marhoon using a mallet and chisel 
9. Close of hands hammering marble
10. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Salem al-Marhoon, Omani artist:
“I am participating with a sculpture in Arabic Calligraphy of the Almighty Allah word. The philosophy of the work is that the Arabic calligraphy is always with (two dimensions) height and width. So I try my best to keep the Arabic Calligraphy with three dimensions, because if calligraphy is made in different directions and in different styles, it always gives good results, and we are impressed of its results.”

11. Martin Chessler, artist, at his artwork
12. Another rtist taking measurement
13. SOUNDBITE (English) Martin Chessler, German artist: 
“We really enjoy it. It's the first time this stone symposium in Salalah. So, it’s still..not everything is perfect, but it's super nice. It's a bit chaotic, what (which) I like. It's about a lot of improvisation, so that's also how I work with my stone. I had an idea, kind of, like I had an idea of the direction, but not the clear vision of the stone. That's also, I think, quite different to all other sculptures here.”

14. Artists near their artwork
15. Wide of symposium venue
STORYLINE:
Under the blazing Omani sun, 25 artists transformed large blocks of white stone and marble to sculptures, each bringing a perspective, and a distinct style. 

They're participating in the Dhofar Sculpture Festival, an event bringing the viewer and artist together through live demonstrations of the craft. 

Visitors had the opportunity to see first-hand the process of creating a sculpture from initial concept to carving and shaping the stone until it represents the artist's final work.  

Jordanian artist Diala al-Daghlise carved a large black of marble using a power grinder and protective gear. 

Mainly a metal artist, she said working with stone for the first time was difficult, yet exciting. 

“It requires physical strength, but also thinking, engineering, and calculations," she explained. 

Omani artist Salem al-Marhoon used a mallet and chisel to carve an Arabic calligraphy sculpture featuring the word 'Allah'.

The contributing artists come from different countries, and the festival aims to be a platform for sharing of expertise. 

The Dhofar Sculpture Festival continues in Salalah until 3 September.

AP video by Dani Noureddine

recentItems.title: After nearly three years of war, Gaza residents lack access to glasses and eye care materials
recentItems.description:
(4 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Khan Younis, Southern Gaza Strip – 2 September 2026
1. Mid of displaced Palestinian, Raed al-Abadi, putting on his broken glasses before lens falls off 
2. Various of Raed al-Abadi showing his broken glasses 
3. Raed al-Abadi trying to fix lens of broken glasses  
4. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Raed al-Abadi, displaced Palestinian: ++PART OVERLAID++
”I have been wearing glasses for 30 years. My eyesight is getting weaker with each passing year. The glass is broken and I am unable to buy a new one. Glasses are expensive. Do we only need food and water? We also need glasses. We need to see, read, read the Quran, cell phones. Nothing works without it.”
5. Raed al-Abadi trying to fix lens of broken glasses  

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Khan Younis, Southern Gaza Strip – 31 August 2026 
6. Various of optician cutting lens and installing it into frame
7. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Ahmad Abu Quta, optician: ++PART OVERLAID++
”There is a shortage in the entry of supplies, which has led to a massive surge in prices. Unfortunately people’s glasses and frames were damaged in their homes, or when they were displaced and they wear them damaged or without an arm.”
8. Various of Abu Quta showing broken frame of glasses
9. Various of optical stores and eye examination centers 
STORYLINE:
Nearly three years of war in the Gaza Strip has left the healthcare system in the Palestinian enclave in ruins.

The ongoing conflict has left residents without access to specialized health services, including eye care materials and supplies. 

Due to the constant displacement with hundreds of thousands of Palestinians moving across the enclave several times during the war, some  lost their glasses while others had their pairs damaged. 

With the healthcare system crippled, they now struggle to buy new ones, or get them repaired. 

“My glasses are broken, and I am unable to buy a new pair. Glasses are expensive,” Raed al-Abadi, 67, said, as he tried to fix his broken pair inside his makeshift tent in southern Gaza. 

Al-Abadi has been wearing glasses for over 30 years, and his eyesight gets weaker with each passing year, he said. 

Access to glasses in Gaza has become particularly challenging due to a lack of supplies. 

Many have come up with improvised solutions to repair their damaged glasses because they cannot afford to buy new pair. 

“This is a lot of suffering,” said Soheir al-Abadi, a displaced Palestinian from Beit Lahiya. 

According to optician Ahmed Abu Kouta there is a lack of optical and eyewear supplies across the enclave, forcing some people to wear expired contact lenses. 

“There is a massive shortage of eye care supplies in general," he said.

"There are no frames, lenses. Unfortunately, we have people wearing expired contact lenses from 2021. When I tell them that the contact lenses expired in 2021 unfortunately their response is that they only want to see.”

The Israel-Hamas war has killed more than 73,400 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. 

The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records viewed as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and international organizations. 

It doesn’t distinguish between civilians and militants, but says women and children make up around half of the toll.

AP video produced by: Wafaa Shurafa

recentItems.title: Four prisoners from Lebanon held in Israel released and handed over to the ICRC Friday
recentItems.description:
(4 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS  
Mansouri, Lebanon - 4 September 2026
1. Various of International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) convoy carrying released detainees passing by, showing men inside the vehicles 
2. Woman talking on the phone UPSOUND (Arabic): "My love, my love, we're waiting for you, me, your dad and your brother."
3. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Mahmoud Ayash, brother of detainee Hussein Ayash:
"He called us now, he was with the ICRC, he called us and told us he was released.”
(Reporter asks off camera: What do you want to say?)
“We thank everyone who helped release my brother and I hope all the detainees and prisoners will be released.”
4. Ayash talking to his brother on the phone
5. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Mahmoud Ayash, brother of detainee Hussein Ayash:
“He’s out, congratulations. I hope all our prisoners in Israeli prisons will be released and for all Lebanese citizens to be liberated and for anyone who is being held in the (Israeli) occupation’s prisons to be released. He called us on the phone from inside.”
6. ICRC convoy driving by the Mansouri checkpoint
7. Various of U.N. vehicles driving by Mansouri checkpoint
8. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Ahmed Atwe, relative of detainee Mohammed Juheir: 
“We came here today because there’s a prisoner release, our relative Mohammed Juheir from Naqoura is detained and we want to see if he’s one of the people released. We pray to God he’s with them. He’s been detained for a year, he was captured at sea in Naqoura, he’s a fisherman.”
9. Various of Lebanese army at the Mansouri checkpoint 
STORYLINE:
Four prisoners from Lebanon held in Israel were released and handed over to the International Committee of the Red Cross Friday as part of a deal between the two countries. In return, Lebanon agreed to search for the bodies of Jewish Lebanese citizens who went missing during the country's civil war decades ago.

Dozens of Lebanese prisoners are believed to be held in Israeli detention centers, including civilians as well as Hezbollah militants captured during fighting in southern Lebanon. A total of five detainees are being released under the current deal, all civilians.

The first Lebanese prisoner, identified as Malek Ghazi, was released to the International Committee of the Red Cross and then to the Lebanese army on Thursday.

Associated Press journalists waiting at a checkpoint south of the city of Tyre in southern Lebanon saw a convoy of International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) vehicles heading toward the Naqoura border crossing Friday morning.

Mahmoud Ayash, the brother of prisoner Hussein Ayash, who was waiting there, said his brother had been detained for over two months and had called from the border crossing in Naqoura to say that he had been released and was with the ICRC.

“I hope all our prisoners in Israeli prisons will be released and for all Lebanese citizens to be liberated,” he said.

The ICRC said in a statement that the remaining prisoners had been transferred to it on Friday. The organization called for its teams to be granted access to the remaining prisoners, noting that it has not had access to detainees held in Israel since October 2023.

“Many families in Lebanon are still waiting for answers about the fate of loved ones who may be detained, deceased or otherwise unaccounted for," it said.


Officials said the prisoner release came as a result of U.S. mediation and as a result of ongoing negotiations between Israel and Lebanon.





Another round of talks is expected to take place in Rome later this month.

AP video shot by Mohamad Anouti, AP Production by Malak Harb

recentItems.title: Freddie Mercury would have turned 80 on September 5
recentItems.description:
(4 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Budapest - 8 August 1986
++4:3 MATERIAL++ 
1. Various of birthday party for Roger Taylor, Freddie Mercury in yellow 
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Freddie Mercury, recoding artist: 
(Reporter: "You have a very extrovert stage act by any standards, will you be able to go on with...") 
"You mean I flaunt it?" 
(Reporter: You're over the top!") 
3. Wide shot Mercury at show

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Munich - 22 May 1984
4. STILL IMAGE - Freddie Mercury, singer in British rock-group Queen, shows his plastered leg, while smoking a cigarette in his hotel room in Munich, Germany, on May 22, 1984. (AP Photo/Uwe Lein) ID  25140466561610

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
London - 13 July 1985
5. STILL IMAGE - George Michael, from left, concert promoter Harvey Goldsmith, Bono, Paul McCartney, Bob Geldof, and Freddie Mercury appear during the London Live Aid Famine Relief Concert in London on July 13, 1985. (AP Photo/Joe Schaber, File) ID 25091302716779

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Sydney, Australia - 1985 
6. STILL IMAGE - Singer Freddie Mercury, of the rock group Queen, performs at a concert (AP Photo/Gill Allen, id: 8501010212)

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Cologne - 20 July 1986
7. STILL IMAGE -The lead singer of the band Queen, Freddie Mercury, singing during an open air concert in Cologne, Germany on July 20, 1986. (AP Photo/Marco Arndt; id: 25143547615387)



STORYLINE:
Freddie Mercury, the flamboyant Queen frontman whose commanding stage presence made him one of rock music’s defining performers, would have turned 80 on September 5. 

Mercury died on November 24 in 1991, at his London home, one day after publicly confirming that he had AIDS. He was 45.

More than three decadse after his death, Mercury remains inseparable from such anthems as “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Somebody to Love” and “We Are the Champions.”

Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar, then a British protectorate off the eastern coast of Africa (now part of Tanzania). He spent much of his childhood at school in India, where he studied piano. His family later settled in England, and Mercury studied graphic art and design before pursuing music in London.

Together with guitarist Brian May and drummer Roger Taylor in 1970, he formed the band Queen, later joined by bassist John Deacon. Mercury became one of its chief songwriters, composing hits including “Killer Queen,” “Crazy Little Thing Called Love” and the six-minute “Bohemian Rhapsody.”

Onstage, Mercury turned concerts into exercises in mass participation, strutting in elaborate costumes and leading audiences through call-and-response vocals. Queen’s roughly 20-minute performance at the Live Aid benefit at Wembley Stadium in 1985 is widely acknowledged as the band’s greatest appearance. Mercury also pursued a solo career and collaborated with Spanish soprano Montserrat Caballé on “Barcelona,” the Olympic Games anthem of 1992.

After his death bandmates May, Taylor and Queen manager Jim Beach helped establish the Mercury Phoenix Trust, which has raised millions of pounds for HIV and AIDS programs worldwide. 

Tributes for his 80th birthday include an official celebration in Montreux, Switzerland, and a 30-foot anamorphic mural near Wembley Stadium.

recentItems.title: Louisiana judge rules against NCAA, clearing path for ex-NFL players to join LSU roster
recentItems.description:
(4 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Baton Rouge, Louisiana - 3 September 2026 
++NIGHT SHOTS++
1. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill and district attorney Tony Clayton walking out of court to address reporters
++BLACK FRAMES++
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Liz Murrill, Louisiana Attorney General: 
"I want to congratulate the lawyers here for the players. They came to this court asking for a fair and unbiased forum to decide a grievance that they brought about the way these rules were being applied to them. And they were not getting a fair hearing from the SEC (Southeastern Conference) or the NCAA (National Collegiate Athletic Association) and I think they did work cooperatively together. In fact, you know, you see the bad faith of these organizations in the way that they've approached this issue just with the lawsuit that they filed today against the Board of Supervisors and other officials at LSU (Louisiana State University). They've been incredibly vindictive, they've been very patronizing and dismissive of the players. They continue to say that this is LSU, then blame (coach) Lane Kiffin and everybody else and try to find somebody evil at one school. In fact, these students all went to different schools, they want, they played at different schools, they are, a lot of them are Louisiana people. I mean, they want to continue to play. Many of them won't make money from that. They just want to play because they love the game. So they're looking for they were looking for a fair and honest decision maker to give them a shot. And they got that here today. And so I was glad to see that."
++BLACK FRAMES++
3. SOUNDBITE (English) Tony Clayton, district attorney: 
"I think the ruling stands for the premise that it's about student athletes. It's not about coach Kiffin, it's not about LSU, it's about treating these kids fairly. It's about the fair application. You have got to apply the rules, apply them fairly to everyone. So today, justice was served and justice was served to the SEC. It was served like a cold cup of gumbo. And that judge forced them to eat it. And so the SEC, if you ask me, and the NCAA really hadn't shown any respect for these court's rulings, and today I think this court, this judge made it clear to them. So, those young student athletes can go on with their lives because they did nothing wrong. And so, we'll wait for the next chapter. If they continue to pick on these children, we will continue to be here to fight for them to make sure that the rules are applied fairly. That's all we ask."
++BLACK FRAMES++
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Dae'Quan Wright, former NFL player: 
Reporter (English): "What made you want to come back to LSU?"
Dae'Quan Wright (English): "Really just being with you know the coaches that brought me to (inaudible). I'm familiar with the system. They've been you know real good to me. Great guys, great group of guys so you know, really just that for real."
++BLACK FRAMES++
5. SOUNDBITE (English) Dae'Quan Wright, former NFL player: 
Reporter (English): "What are you most looking forward to about Saturday?"
Dae'Quan Wright (English): "Just putting on a college uniform again and going out there and having fun and embracing my opportunity."
++BLACK FRAMES++
6. SOUNDBITE (English) Dae'Quan Wright, former NFL player: 
Reporter (English): "Hearing (SEC Commissioner) Greg Sankey today saying all those things on the stand, obviously you've been there since this morning, what's going through your mind?"
++BLACK FRAMES++
7. SOUNDBITE (English) Dae'Quan Wright, former NFL player: 
++ENDS ON SOUNDBITE++

recentItems.title: Lenovo previews laptop with rollable screen, crystal-encrusted smartphone
recentItems.description:
(4 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS

Berlin, Germany - 3 September 2026

1. Opening of Lenovo press conference
2. Cutaway of attendee filming with smartphone
3. Cutaway of attendees watching press conference
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Luca Rossi, president of Intelligent Devices Group, Lenovo:
"Project Swan approaches mobility from a different angle. With business laptops, people often face a choice, carry a smaller device that's easier to move with or a larger screen that gives more room to work. Projects Swan asks, why not both? In fact, it's an ultra-portable and lightweight 14-inch notebook concept with an horizontal rollable display. In its compact mode, it gives you a familiar 14- inch display. But when they need more workspace, the screen rolls out horizontally to a 17-inch, landscape display."

5. Wide of Lenovo demo area
6. Pan of Lenovo demo area
7. Various of Project Swan concept laptop with rollable screen
8. Media looking at Project Swan concept laptop
9. Project Swan concept laptop 
10. SOUNDBITE (English) Luca Rossi, president of Intelligent Devices Group, Lenovo:
"It's a fanless 14-inch ultra-thin, ultra-light notebook concept, powered with our friends at Intel. Our vision to have a premium clamshell laptop that is easier to carry, quieter to use, but still uncompromising in productivity, comes to life with this concept. Project AeroBlade re-engineers all the key system components, from chassis to display, to battery, to the thermal architecture, all around mobility and usability. It's under one kilogram, under 10 millimeters thin, about the thickness of a pencil, with whisper quiet operation, even under performing workloads."

11. Attendee looking at Project AeroBlade concept laptop
12. Various of Project AeroBlade concept laptop
13. Wide of Rossi speaking onstage
14. Cutaway of attendee filming with smartphone
15. Cutaway of stage lights 
16. SOUNDBITE (English) Luca Rossi, president of Intelligent Devices Group, Lenovo:
"We are unveiling a new addition to our brilliant collection featuring Crystals by Swarovski, as well as the Motorola Edge 70 Plus and the Moto Watch Ultra. Let me start, I should have something here. This is the razr 70 with Crystals by Swarovski."

17. Various of motorola razr with Crystals by Swarovski
18. Attendee filming motorola razr with Crystals by Swarovski
19. SOUNDBITE (English) Luca Rossi, president of Intelligent Devices Group, Lenovo:
"The moto watch Ultra is our premium smartwatch that allows you to stay connected even when your phone is not. And it's the first moto watch with LTE and eSIM. It's made for people who want a wearable that looks great, works more independently, delivers smarter health insights, and of course, is built to last. For health and fitness, it brings advanced tracking with polar integration, from running guidance to sleep, heart rate, stress, recovery insights. The goal is simple, help people understand their body better."

20. Various of moto watch ultra on display
21. Various of exhibitor demonstrating moto watch ultra
22. Executives posing for photos onstage after press conference
23. Wide of people leaving after press conference
STORYLINE:
LEADIN:

As Berlin’s IFA consumer electronics show gets underway, China-based Lenovo has unveiled a concept laptop with a rollable screen.

It's also announced a crystal-encrusted foldable smartphone. 

STORYLINE:

Created for people who want a laptop with a larger working space, this new concept laptop by Lenovo, named “Project Swan”, explores a future where workspaces expand when users need it.
